In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel, non-invasive biomarkers that can be applied for patient selection for ICI.
the role of the extracellular matrix ( ECM ) in cancer and the development of non-invasive biomarkers for the diagnosis of cancer.
identifying biomarkers for predicting treatment response and outcomes in patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the biomarker profile of PRO-C3, C3M, C4M, C3MC3M and VICM are associated with treatment response and survival outcome in metastatic melanomas treated with ipilimumab.

the biomarkers of collagen turnover and citrullination of vimentin were associated with response, and survival in metastatic melanma patients treated with ICI, but the association was not strong enough to be used as a predictive biomarker.
the biomarkers of ECM remodeling and tissue remodeling are associated with response and overall survival in metastatic melanomas patients treated with ICI.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a reactive stroma, quantified in pre- and on-treatment serum, is associated with response and overall survival in melanoma patients treated by immune checkpoint inhibition.
the ECM is an integral part of the tumor microenvironment and can be quantified with non-invasive biomarkers in serum.
the biomarker signature is predictive for survival in metastatic melanomas treated with IPI and the biomarker levels are dynamic and change during treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use non-invasive biomarkers of collagen turnover to predict response to IPI in melanoma patients.
the ECM is a potential biomarker for treatment response in melanoma and possibly in other ICI-treated cancers.
the ECM is a dynamic and important player in the immune system.
